title: Runtime gates fail on QEMU 10.0.13: virtio-net queue size is 1024, check requires 256.
body:
Hi Gregory,

I ran an independent review of Ginux at commit d11c126a (with AI-assisted analysis, under my direction) and found one reproducible issue I thought worth sharing first.

On QEMU v10.0.13 (Debian), all runtime gates fail at boot because verify_network_queue_rejections requires receive_queue_size == 256, while the device reports 1024. In the QEMU source, virtio_add_queue in v10.0.13 forces queue_size = VIRTQUEUE_MAX_SIZE ("Always set to max queue size for qemu <11.1"); v10.0.10, v10.0.12 and v10.1.0 honor the requested size (256). Setting rx_queue_size=256 has no effect on v10.0.13.

The functional init path accepts any power of two >= 8, so only the calibration assertion fails. Possible fixes: pin/check the QEMU version in make doctor, or accept a range in that assertion.

Thanks for the open-source work,
[Abdelhafid DJIDEL]

title: Tracking: technical criticism of Ginux collected from public reviews
body:
## What this is

This issue collects, in one place, the technical criticism of Ginux that has been raised publicly (a kernel developer's review, Hacker News discussion, and press and blog coverage). It also includes a few points found while checking the project's own claims. Each point was checked against the code at `main` commit [`1852455`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267), and only points that held up are listed. Links are permalinks to that commit.

Most items map onto the hardening plan in [`docs/FEEDBACK-HARDENING-RESEARCH.md`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/FEEDBACK-HARDENING-RESEARCH.md) (stages F0–F7, added in #3), so this is meant to complement that plan with concrete code locations, not duplicate it. The maintainer has said fixes for the original review are in progress, so some items may already be addressed by the time you read this. Please tick or close them as they land, or split any item into its own issue if that's easier to discuss.

**Status update (31 Oct 2026):** checked against `main` at [`22d20a6`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/commit/22d20a63544855148992e20d27d71c0e42f319d2) after [#7](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/7) and [#8](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/8) merged, plus open [#9](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/9), [#10](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/10) and [#11](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/11). Each item now has two sub-boxes: one for when a PR addresses it and one for when that fix is merged to main. The main box is ticked only when the item is fully resolved on main. Evidence links below still point at the original commit `1852455`.

Thanks for publishing the code, plan and artifacts openly, which made this kind of review possible.

---

## Security / entry path

- [x] **NMI and #MC have no IST stack, so they can run on a user-controlled RSP in the SYSCALL entry window.** Stage: **F1**.
  - [x] In a PR: [#7](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/7)
  - [x] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): Fixed: per-CPU guarded IST stacks for NMI, #DF and #MC (`cpu/architecture.rs`).

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - Only #DF (vector 8) gets an IST: [`cpu.rs#L29`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L29) (`DOUBLE_FAULT_IST = 1`), [`cpu.rs#L8814-L8820`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L8814-L8820) (only `TSS.interrupt_stacks[0]` set), [`cpu.rs#L8860-L8867`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L8860-L8867) (`install_idt`: `ist = if vector == 8 { DOUBLE_FAULT_IST } else { 0 }`). [`cpu.rs#L8876-L8893`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L8876-L8893) asserts this layout.
  - Entry window: [`cpu.rs#L2233-L2240`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L2233-L2240). `ginux_linux_syscall_entry` runs `cli; clac; cld` and saves user state before `mov rsp, [user_return_stack]`, so an NMI/#MC here (CPL0→CPL0, IST 0) pushes its frame at the user RSP.
  - NMI/#MC go to `ginux_fatal_exception_common` ([`#L1998`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L1998), [`#L2016`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L2016), [`#L2031-L2068`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L2031-L2068)), which pushes 15 more GPRs and calls Rust on that stack.
  - Mitigating today: ring 0 runs with IF=0; NMI/#MC are already fatal; SMAP is on ([`lib.rs#L498-L499`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/lib.rs#L498-L499)), so a user-page RSP turns into #PF → #DF on IST1. A writable supervisor RSP still gets ~160 bytes written before the halt.

  **Suggested direction:** separate guarded IST stacks for NMI, #MC, #DF and #DB (like Linux's `IST_INDEX_*`), per-CPU from the start so F6 doesn't redo them; update `exception_gates_are_valid()`; decide nested-NMI semantics; add a QEMU test that injects an NMI (monitor `nmi`) while userspace loops on `syscall`.
  </details>

One additional entry-path finding is being reported privately.

## User memory access

- [x] **User copies have no fault recovery, and runtime validation can trust software bookkeeping over the hardware page tables.** Stage: **F2**.
  - [x] In a PR: [#7](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/7)
  - [x] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): Fixed: `ginux_raw_copy_{from,to}_user` with exception fixups that return EFAULT. The `frame.is_some()` branch is still there but no longer unsafe.

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - Validate-then-dereference: `copy_from_linux_user` / `copy_to_linux_user` at [`cpu.rs#L37810-L37824`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L37810-L37824) and [`cpu.rs#L40698-L40714`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L40698-L40714) check the range in software, then dereference inside `stac`/`clac`.
  - No fixup: a kernel-mode #PF only tries `kernel_linux_cow_fault_handler` ([`cpu.rs#L2031-L2068`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L2031-L2068)), which accepts only present+write COW faults ([`cpu.rs#L43947-L43962`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L43947-L43962)). Anything else halts via `fatal_exception_handler` ([`cpu.rs#L44296-L44321`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L44296-L44321)). No exception table exists.
  - Two validators: `linux_user_range_covered` ([`cpu.rs#L37560-L37639`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L37560-L37639)) uses software region bookkeeping unless `LINUX_RUNTIME_MODE` is set.
  - Fallback: in `materialize_linux_runtime_user_range` ([`cpu.rs#L37661-L37691`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L37661-L37691)), when the real PTE check `current_linux_range_mapped` ([`address_space.rs#L5236-L5262`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/address_space.rs#L5236-L5262)) fails but `page.frame.is_some()`, the page is accepted without being mapped. Safety relies on invariants held in other modules.
  - `with_supervisor_user_access` is also used at 11 other sites in `cpu.rs` and 17 in `address_space.rs`. `copy_linux_c_string` ([`cpu.rs#L37826-L37839`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L37826-L37839)) re-validates per byte.

  **Suggested direction:** a small assembly user-access module (`copy_{from,to}_user`, `strncpy_from_user`, `get/put_user`, futex atomics) with exception-table fixups returning bytes not copied (`clac` on the fixup path); keep a cheap `access_ok` check and let hardware be the final authority; remove or fix the `frame.is_some()` branch; Linux partial-copy/`-EFAULT` semantics; tests for unmapped, non-canonical, kernel-half, read-only, guard-page and cross-page buffers, plus a `munmap` race during a large `read`.
  </details>

## Architecture: global state, single CPU, `cpu.rs` size

- [ ] **Signal and process state lives in mutable globals selected per execution instance; this can't survive SMP.** Stage: **F3** (then F6).
  - [x] In a PR: [#7](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/7)
  - [x] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): Partly: every global is now classified and checked by `check-writable-globals.sh`, but state is still in `Banked*` statics, not process/thread objects.

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - Approx. counts (`rg`, `kernel/src`): ~604 `static` items (~432 in `cpu.rs`), 67 `static mut`, ~175 atomic statics, 336 `Banked*` statics.
  - Signal globals: [`cpu.rs#L1771-L1794`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L1771-L1794), [`cpu.rs#L1914-L1923`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L1914-L1923) (`static mut LINUX_USER_RSP/RIP/RFLAGS`, `LINUX_SIGNAL_*`, used by entry asm), [`cpu.rs#L1512-L1523`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L1512-L1523) (per-thread masks as a global array).
  - `Banked*` types ([`cpu.rs#L999-L1083`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L999-L1083)) pick a bank via global `LINUX_EXECUTION_INSTANCE`; state is copied in/out on process switch ([`cpu.rs#L13929-L14040`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L13929-L14040)).

  **Suggested direction:** commit the inventory as a script with a classification column that fails CI on new unclassified globals; migrate signal state into process/thread objects first.
  </details>

- [ ] **Exclusion relies on a single CPU with interrupts off; there are no locks, and `SAFETY:` comments depend on this.** Stage: **F4** (then F6).
  - [x] In a PR: [#7](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/7), [#8](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/8)
  - [x] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): Mostly: ranked spinlocks and SMP landed, but all kernel entry still goes through one coarse `KERNEL_ENTRY_LOCK`, and a few `SAFETY:` comments still cite the bootstrap CPU.

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - Entry stubs start with `cli` ([`cpu.rs#L2031-L2033`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L2031-L2033), [`#L2233-L2236`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L2233-L2236)); interrupts open only in explicit windows ([`pci.rs#L1042-L1055`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/pci.rs#L1042-L1055), [`timer.rs#L327-L334`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/timer.rs#L327-L334)).
  - No spinlock/mutex types in `kernel/src`. SAFETY comments cite the single bootstrap processor: [`scheduler.rs#L1153-L1155`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/scheduler.rs#L1153-L1155), [`linux_process.rs#L35-L40`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/linux_process.rs#L35-L40), [`pci.rs#L518-L521`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/pci.rs#L518-L521).
  - No AP startup; [`docs/PERFORMANCE.md`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/PERFORMANCE.md) is honest that there's no SMP claim.

  **Suggested direction:** one IRQ-safe spinlock type and a lock-order doc before converting subsystems; replace "single bootstrap processor" justifications with the lock that actually provides exclusion (grep gives a ready to-do list).
  </details>

- [ ] **`kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` is 44,324 lines and holds non-arch Linux personality policy.** Stage: **F5**.
  - [x] In a PR: [#7](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/7), [#9](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/9)
  - [ ] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): Partly: about 8k lines moved into `cpu/`, but `cpu.rs` is still 42,876 lines. #9 moves a little more.

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - [`cpu.rs`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs): ~1,037 top-level fns (~609 `linux_*`), ~432 statics, GDT/TSS/IDT, entry asm, user copy, plus sockets, signals, exec, mmap, epoll, futex, `/proc`.
  - `linux_syscall_handler` spans [`cpu.rs#L8990`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs#L8990) to ~L10415 (~1,400 lines).

  **Suggested direction:** extract mechanical parts first (descriptor tables, entry asm, user access, MSRs) so F1/F2 fixes land in small files; then move personality code out of `arch/` and turn the syscall handler into a dispatch table.
  </details>

## Rust `unsafe` / lint coverage

- [ ] **`unsafe` isn't confined to documented boundaries (~1,060 blocks, 115 SAFETY comments, no inventory), and `make check` never runs clippy on `ginux-kernel`.** Stage: **F5** (deliverable at [`FEEDBACK-HARDENING-RESEARCH.md#L195`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/FEEDBACK-HARDENING-RESEARCH.md#L195)), overlaps F3.
  - [x] In a PR: [#9](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/9)
  - [ ] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): Partly, in #9 only: kernel clippy plus an unsafe-count cap. No `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` lint or inventory yet.

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - Goal stated in [`ARCHITECTURE.md#L25`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/ARCHITECTURE.md#L25) and inventory listed as a deliverable at [`#L283`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/ARCHITECTURE.md#L283); no inventory file exists.
  - Approx. `unsafe {` blocks: `address_space.rs` 301 (11 SAFETY), `linux_socket.rs` 142 (0), `cpu.rs` 140 (31). 14,658 lines of hand-written `.S`; `address_space.rs` includes 12 asm programs ([`#L47-L58`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/address_space.rs#L47-L58)).
  - Crate-wide `#![allow(static_mut_refs)]`: [`lib.rs#L1`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/lib.rs#L1), [`linux_socket.rs#L1`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/linux_socket.rs#L1); e.g. `SLOTS` ([`#L188`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/linux_socket.rs#L188)) read in bare unsafe at [`#L205-L221`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/linux_socket.rs#L205-L221).
  - [`Makefile#L239-L265`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/Makefile#L239-L265) runs clippy for 15 packages but not `ginux-kernel` (from reading the Makefile; not run locally). No `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` / `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` lints enabled.

  **Suggested direction:** add `ginux-kernel` to `make check` with a baseline of explicit allows, then ratchet; enable `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` and `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` and use the count as the inventory metric; replace `allow(static_mut_refs)` with `&raw` or wrapper types; separate test-fixture asm from production asm.
  </details>

## Testing / CI

- [ ] **`make test` is a known failure, there's no CI, and the kernel crate has zero unit tests (verification is mostly serial-log matching).** Stage: **F0** and **F7**. Related: #4.
  - [x] In a PR: [#9](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/9)
  - [ ] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): In #9 only: a GitHub Actions workflow and a host-tested `kernel-policy` crate. Virtio fix for #4 is in #10.

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - Known red: [`README.md#L233-L236`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/README.md#L233-L236), [`docs/PERFORMANCE.md#L138-L142`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/PERFORMANCE.md#L138-L142), [paper](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/paper/ginux-ai-systems-report.tex#L664-L669). Failing probe isn't named or tracked; nearest marker [`lib.rs#L2074`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/lib.rs#L2074). `make gate` ends in `make test` ([`Makefile#L270`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/Makefile#L270)), so it can't pass.
  - No `.github/` or other CI; [`STABILITY-AUDIT.md#L82-L83`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/STABILITY-AUDIT.md#L82-L83) recorded a pass that later regressed unnoticed.
  - 53 `#[test]`s in `crates/*`, 0 in `kernel/`. [`tests/qemu/boot.sh`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/tests/qemu/boot.sh): 4,163 lines, ~1,100 grep checks on serial output.
  - Self-tests in every boot ([`lib.rs#L247-L258`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/lib.rs#L247-L258)); test modes via runtime `if cfg!(...)` ([`#L508`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/lib.rs#L508), [`#L1086`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/lib.rs#L1086), [`#L1159`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/kernel/src/lib.rs#L1159)), so probe code and fixture asm are always linked.
  - #4 (https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/issues/4) shows a boot check failing on QEMU 10.0.13 due to a fixed virtio-net queue size expectation, the kind of drift CI would catch.

  **Suggested direction:** track the failing post-`execve()` probe and mark it expected-fail so the gate goes green; minimal GitHub Actions running `make check` and `make test`; host-side `#[cfg(test)]` unit tests for parsers and syscall decoding; move self-tests out of production boot and use `#[cfg(feature)]`. Consider "CI green on the baseline tag" as an F0 acceptance criterion.
  </details>

## Compatibility claims

- [ ] **The compatibility ledger's 82 "Complete" includes 17 ENOSYS stubs, and some socket calls marked Complete contradict the matrix's own limits.** Stage: **F0** (claim confirmation) / **F7** (re-counted totals).
  - [x] In a PR: [#9](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/9), [#11](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/pull/11)
  - [ ] Merged to main
  - Status (31 Oct): In #9/#11 only: the 17 ENOSYS stubs move to Unsupported and 12 socket calls to Partial.

  <details><summary>Evidence and suggested direction</summary>

  - Headline totals: [`LINUX-COMPATIBILITY.md#L45`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/LINUX-COMPATIBILITY.md#L45); "Complete" requires positive, negative and edge-case tests ([`#L35`](https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux/blob/1852455ec05ff34b288dbd41e224e700b82bd267/docs/LINUX-COMPATIBILITY.md#L35)).

title: Harden kernel entry, state ownership, and SMP operation
body:
## Summary

This PR turns external kernel-review feedback into an eleven-gate HDAE hardening experiment. It hardens privilege entry and userspace access, replaces ambient global state with explicit ownership, decomposes the x86-64 implementation, adds synchronization and SMP operation, and requalifies the complete system.

## Completed gates

1. **Baseline and claim reproduction** — preserved the published baseline, reproduced each review claim with deterministic evidence, and inventoried writable global state.
2. **Privilege-entry hardening** — moved `SYSCALL` entry onto trusted per-CPU state before stack use, added guarded NMI/double-fault/machine-check ISTs, and validated return state.
3. **Fault-recovering userspace access** — added recoverable user-copy primitives so invalid userspace pointers return faults instead of panicking the kernel.
4. **Global-state classification** — classified every writable global by owner, lifetime, synchronization, teardown, and migration disposition, with architecture enforcement.
5. **Runtime-state ownership** — consolidated domain, scheduler, process, socket, signal, keyring, and AIO state under explicit lifecycle owners.
6. **Platform/service ownership** — consolidated network, storage, image, memory, paging, interrupt, timer, and service state under explicit host, domain, or per-CPU owners.
7. **x86-64 decomposition** — split the former monolithic CPU module into architecture, ABI, execution, syscall, time, futex, polling, and signal components while preserving behavior.
8. **Synchronization and SMP readiness** — added ranked spinlocks and IRQ-safe locks, protected the frame allocator, enforced lock ordering, and audited interrupt masking.
9. **SMP operation** — added AP discovery/startup, per-CPU protected state and stacks, IPIs, TLB shootdowns, cross-CPU Linux execution, and 1/2/4-vCPU qualification; QEMU tests now default to two vCPUs.
10. **Qualification and comparison** — passed the frozen static, ABI, storage, OCI, Rocky, package-network, multi-domain, SMP, stress, and benchmark matrix and preserved the results and limitations.
11. **Matched topology benchmarks** — measured Rocky on Linux and Ginux at 1, 2, and 4 vCPUs with fixed and scaled thread counts using the same pinned sysbench binary. Two benchmark-discovered correctness failures were fixed in bounded follow-up gates: shared-writable-page TLB coherence (11.5) and exact cross-thread register restoration (11.6).

## Validation

The completed qualification includes:

- `make check`
- `make architecture-check`
- deterministic feedback reproduction
- full QEMU boot and Linux ABI suites
- 1-, 2-, and 4-vCPU SMP tests plus repeated 2-vCPU stress runs
- storage, OCI cache, Rocky systemd, controller responsiveness, `dnf`, and multi-domain tests
- matched Linux/Ginux topology benchmarks with nine samples per sysbench cell and three samples per boot cell

Detailed qualification evidence is recorded in `docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-10-QUALIFICATION.md`. The topology comparison is in `docs/feedback-hardening/GATE-11-TOPOLOGY-BENCHMARKS.md`, with reduced TSV evidence under `docs/feedback-hardening/gate-11-results/` and the complete gate history under `hdae/gates-done/`.

## Matched topology benchmark results

Environment: Rocky Linux 10 userspace, QEMU 10.1.2 x86-64 TCG on Apple Silicon, Q35, 2 GiB RAM, and an identical pinned sysbench binary on both kernels. Throughput ratios are Ginux/Linux; mutex ratios use Linux/Ginux because lower time is better. A value above `1.0x` favors Ginux.

### Fixed at one workload thread

| vCPUs | CPU | Memory | Threads | Mutex |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1.192x | 1.194x | 0.977x | 1.104x |
| 2 | 1.006x | 1.110x | 0.311x | 1.055x |
| 4 | 1.029x | 1.121x | 0.324x | 1.066x |

### Workload threads scaled with vCPUs

| vCPUs/threads | CPU | Memory | Threads | Mutex |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1/1 | 1.192x | 1.194x | 0.977x | 1.104x |
| 2/2 | 1.278x | 1.033x | 0.863x | 0.781x |
| 4/4 | 0.658x | 0.839x | 0.085x | 0.425x |

CPU and memory are competitive at one and two vCPUs in this translated environment. Four-thread results expose the principal remaining limitation: Ginux reaches 0.658x Linux CPU throughput, 0.839x memory throughput, 0.085x thread-yield throughput, and 0.425x favorable mutex performance. This is a measured scheduling and yield scalability gap, not a claim of native-hardware or general kernel performance.

Boot medians were 46.721/14.517 seconds at one vCPU, 34.268/16.032 seconds at two, and 31.825/15.940 seconds at four for Rocky on Linux/Ginux respectively. These are complete-path observations rather than a kernel-speed comparison because the firmware, kernel, initramfs, storage, and userspace-startup paths differ.

## Scope

This closes the defined feedback-hardening research gates. It does not claim production security, complete Linux compatibility, arbitrary hardware support, native-hardware performance, or unconstrained SMP scalability.

title: TLS 1.3 client RNG is seeded solely from the RTC boot second — full session decryption from a passive capture (ephemeral key replayed across all connections)
body:
## Summary

The registry TLS client in `services/network/src/registry.rs` seeds its `ChaCha8Rng` **exclusively from the RTC boot timestamp (second resolution)**, and re-seeds it identically for every connection of a pull:

- `seed()` (registry.rs:1094-1102): all 32 seed bytes are `unix_time * (1..=4)` words
- `https_get` (registry.rs:1011-1012) constructs `Provider { rng: ChaCha8Rng::from_seed(seed()) }` per request
- the clock is stored once at boot (registry.rs:85-87) and never updated

Because embedded-tls draws the ClientHello random **and then the P-256 ephemeral secret** from that one stream, **every TLS connection of a pull emits the identical client_random and the identical ephemeral key**.

## Impact

From a **passive capture of one boot's pull** we reproduced:

1. 8 TLS connections (registry-1.docker.io, auth.docker.io, CloudFront) — one byte-identical client_random and key share
2. brute-forcing the boot second recovered the seed in **905 candidates**
3. the derived scalar reproduces the observed key_share public key
4. the server handshake flight (EncryptedExtensions/Certificate/CertificateVerify/Finished) **and application data** (the `HTTP/1.1 401` + `www-authenticate: Bearer realm=...` response) were decrypted **offline, without the server certificate**

An active on-path attacker can relay the genuine certificate flight and then forge application-data records. With by-tag pulls (the default everywhere) this yields attacker-chosen image content flowing into the ring-0 tar/inflate parsers.

## Suggested fix

Seed all crypto RNG from `RDSEED`/`RDRAND` (+ a time/jitter mix-in), never derive TLS key material from RTC alone, and re-seed per connection.

---
*Found with the [rust-in-peace](https://habr.com/ru/articles/1089374/) methodology and the [reproof](https://github.com/scadastrangelove/reproof) multi-lens pipeline (seed-diverse static passes + adversarial verification + dynamic PoCs on a QEMU rig). The name says G is for GPT — from our bench these particular finds arrive courtesy of **K for Kimi** and **G for GLM**, so the alphabet is converging from both sides. Full PoC harnesses and captures available on request.*

title: Digest-pinned image references never verify the top-level manifest body (@sha256: pin is unused)
body:
## Summary

For a digest-pinned reference (`image@sha256:X`), the pin only builds the URL path (`/v2/<repo>/manifests/sha256:X`, selector written via `write_manifest_path`). The fetched top-level body is **never checked against X**:

- the only digest verifications in `pull()` (services/network/src/registry.rs:243-303) are the sub-manifest vs the index's own descriptor (:297-298), the config (:376-383), and the layers
- whether the top-level body is an index or a manifest, the pin is decorative

A malicious or compromised registry can serve any self-consistent manifest+layers chain under a pinned digest path.

## Impact

This silently nullifies by-digest pinning — the standard mitigation for the weak-RNG issue (see the TLS RNG report). Fixing the RNG without verifying the top-level digest leaves the pull anchored to nothing. `profiles/rocky-10-system-v0/image.env` already carries a digest pin under the belief it binds (host-side today).

## Suggested fix

After fetching the top-level manifest body, verify `sha256(body) == pin` when the reference is digest-pinned.

title: Unbounded PAX-header recursion in the OCI tar parser — kernel panic from a ~9 KB layer
body:
## Summary

`parse_entry` (crates/oci/src/lib.rs:712-724) recurses into the next 512-byte header for every PAX `x` entry with **no depth parameter**, and `parse_pax_overrides` accepts an empty payload. `TAR_MAX_ENTRIES` (32768) counts returned entries, not chain depth, so N chained PAX headers = N nested stack frames for 1 counted entry.

`Rootfs::parse` runs in ring 0 from `install_published_layers` (kernel/src/image_store.rs:451, and the sibling site kernel/src/published_rootfs.rs:99).

## Repro (dynamic, on a QEMU rig)

A single 9 KB gzip layer containing 4000 chained empty PAX headers + one real entry, delivered as a warm-cache image:

```
ginux: checking OCI cache docker.io/library/alpine:latest
ginux: OCI cache hit (1 layer)
GINUX_KERNEL_PANIC
```

The whole machine panics at domain start from a ~9 KB hostile layer. (Repeats a crate-level repro: the unmodified `ginux_oci::Rootfs::parse` overflows a 256 KiB stack at ~1000 headers in a release profile.)

Note the delivery vehicle: the on-volume OCI cache is integrity-only (keyless SHA-256, crates/volume-format), so a block-device writer can plant such a layer offline with zero network — worth a hardening pass of its own.

## Suggested fix

Convert the PAX-chain walk to iteration or add an explicit depth cap (e.g. 32).

title: Directory whiteouts (.wh.<name>) do not hide the subtree — deleted files resurrect from lower layers
body:
## Summary

A directory whiteout in a derived layer removes only the exact path, not the subtree:

- crates/oci/src/lib.rs:697-703 (`whiteout_hides`) matches `dir+name` exactly
- kernel/src/published_rootfs.rs:251 tombstones the exact path; `remove_index_children` (:461-482) exists but is invoked only for `.wh..wh..opq`

The OCI layer spec deletes the directory **and all children**; here children of a whited-out directory stay resolvable by full path.

## Repro (dynamic)

Two-layer warm-cache image: base layer contains `secret/key`; upper layer contains `.wh.secret`. On the booted domain:

```
ginux: OCI cache hit (2 layers)
ginux: OCI image ready
ginux: entering configured Linux init
TOPSECRET-BASE-LAYER-KEY-G04      <-- open("/secret/key") succeeded and printed the base-layer content
```

## Impact

Content an image author removed in an update layer (scrubbed secrets, replaced-vulnerable binaries) silently reappears — a classic patch-defeat / data-resurrection pattern for derived images.

## Suggested fix

Reuse the existing `remove_index_children` for plain directory whiteouts, not just opaque markers.

title: Per-domain memory limits are not enforced (memory_limit_mib unused; both mmap and shmget bypass it)
body:
## Summary

The advertised per-domain memory limit is not connected to any allocator:

- `memory_limit_mib` (kernel/src/domain.rs:127) has zero consumers outside domain.rs
- every Linux-runtime allocation is charged `FrameOwner::KERNEL` against the one global frame pool (anon mmap cpu.rs:20151+, stack growth cpu.rs:42306+, tmpfs linux_tmpfs.rs, SysV shm linux_sysv_ipc.rs:383+)
- default `RLIMIT_AS = u64::MAX` (cpu.rs:36246-36256) neuters the address-space guard

This matches STABILITY-AUDIT.md S2 ("allocations are not yet charged to domains") — reporting it because the config knob suggests enforcement that does not exist.

## Repro (dynamic, two different syscall families)

1. Domain configured with `memory-mib=8`; an mmap+touch loop allocated and touched **576+ MiB** (72x the knob)
2. A `shmget` loop (no SHMMAX-style cap) allocated **577 MiB** of KERNEL-owned frames from one domain vs `DOMAIN_FRAME_LIMIT` 768 KiB (~770x) before global-pool exhaustion

Either way one domain starves every other domain and the kernel.

## Suggested fix

title: Blocking socket syscalls busy-wait for a guest-chosen SO_RCVTIMEO while holding kernel_entry_lock
body:
## Summary

`recv_message_blocking` (kernel/src/linux_socket.rs:1681-1697) implements blocking as

```rust
let limit = timeout_poll_limit(slot, TimeoutOption::Receive).unwrap_or(BLOCKING_POLL_LIMIT);
for _ in 0..limit {
    match recv_message(slot, output, peek_only) {
        Err(Error::WouldBlock | Error::InProgress) => core::hint::spin_loop(),
        result => return result,
    }
}
```

`limit` derives from the guest-set `SO_RCVTIMEO` (setsockopt cpu.rs:28727), and the loop runs on the syscall path under `kernel_entry_lock`. A guest that sets a very large timeout and issues a blocking recv/send/accept with no data available spins the big lock for a guest-chosen duration. (Same class, smaller: the getrandom fill loop in linux_random.rs:91 has no length cap.)

Dynamic confirmation is pending (our first oracle faulted in socket setup before reaching the spin), but the code shape is unambiguous.

## Impact

One unprivileged domain process stalls the whole host (all CPUs serialize on the entry lock) for an attacker-chosen time.

## Suggested fix

Dequeue/deschedule instead of busy-waiting, or bound the poll budget and drop the lock between iterations.

title: Test reserved volume header bytes with a valid digest

### Problem

`ginux_volume_format::decode` rejects a sector whose reserved header bytes
(`RESERVED_OFFSET..HEADER_SIZE`, bytes 64..72) are nonzero. No test covers that
guard. The existing corruption test changes a byte without recomputing the
digest, so the SHA-256 check rejects the sector before the reserved bytes
matter. With the guard removed (and the then-unused `RESERVED_OFFSET` constant
with it), `cargo fmt --all -- --check`,
`cargo clippy --package ginux-volume-format -- -D warnings` and
`cargo test --package ginux-volume-format` all still pass.

### Solution

One test in the existing `mod tests` of `crates/volume-format/src/lib.rs`.
For each reserved offset it sets the byte to 1, recomputes the digest with
`digest_sector`, and asserts `decode` returns `None`. It first asserts the
unmodified committed sector decodes. No production code changes.

The per-offset pattern is adapted from
[aien-dev/aienux `store_v1_negative.rs` at edac0f1b](https://github.com/aien-dev/aienux/blob/edac0f1b14dcc469fceb18783aa92ff6d92645b2/crates/aienos-kernel/tests/store_v1_negative.rs#L315-L324)

## Summary

`process_vm_readv/writev` (kernel/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs:20562-20700) authorize via ptrace/same-credential checks, but the imported `LinuxActiveImageMapping` (kernel/src/linux_process.rs:3006-3130) **drops the hardware page-table secret bit** (`memfd_secret` mappings), and the remote copy then goes straight through the frame direct map with no secret check.

Preserve the `secret` flag in `LinuxActiveImageMapping` and reject secret pages in every remote-copy primitive.

title: mprotect(PROT_READ) leaves a stale writable TLB on sibling CPUs — write succeeds after the syscall returns (SMP)
body:
## Summary

The read-only fast path of `mprotect` (`protect_current_linux_range_read_only`, kernel/src/address_space.rs:3436-3478) clears WRITABLE in the shared PTE but performs only a **local** `invlpg`. ## Repro (dynamic, QEMU, 2 vCPU — reproduced twice)

Thread pinned to CPU 0 called `mprotect(PROT_READ)` on a warmed page; a syscall-free sibling on CPU 1 **wrote the page successfully after mprotect returned** (active-image page 0x405000). Violates same-process protection/RELRO semantics; the acknowledged cross-CPU invalidation mechanism exists (kernel/src/arch/x86_64/smp.rs:505-544) but is not used on this path.

## Suggested fix

Use the acknowledged remote-shootdown path for permission revocation before returning success.

## Summary

`with_runtime_volume` (kernel/src/lib.rs:4540-4574) calls `backend.finish()` and `translation.finish()`, then **scrubs and releases the DMA frame unconditionally**, before evaluating the combined result. title: Failed IOMMU activation rollback releases translation tables it may still be walking
body:
## Summary

After a partial IOMMU activation failure, `rollback_activation` (kernel/src/arch/x86_64/iommu.rs:462-525) ignores every disable/root-clear/status result; `DeviceTranslationProfile::activate` then retires the inactive hierarchy, **scrubbing and releasing all six translation-table frames even when rollback failed**. Propagate rollback failure; keep table leases quarantined until the translation is proven inactive.

title: Drive the registry network clock from the calibrated TSC
body:
## Summary

Under KVM, OCI registry pulls fail with "OCI registry TCP connection failed" whenever the registry is more than about 200 ms away. The registry service derives smoltcp time from a poll counter (1024 polls per millisecond) and bounds every wait at 25M polls. On a fast host that clock runs about 140x real time, so TCP gives up before the SYN-ACK arrives. TCG hides it because emulated polls are slow.

This PR gives native services a real clock and fixes a Linux-host harness bug found on the way.

- Native operation 39 returns the kernel-calibrated TSC frequency, the same source the Linux clock profile uses. No capability is required.
- The registry service calls it once per session and reads RDTSC per poll. A call per poll would exhaust the 23-call service budget.
- One monotonic session clock replaces the per-connection tick, which restarted at zero after DNS had advanced the interface clock.
- Waits are bounded by the same 24.4 s, now in time rather than polls. Each wait still checks the socket before the deadline on every poll.
- DNS refreshes the interface time before starting a query, since smoltcp stamps the query timeout from the last poll.
- If the kernel reports the frequency unavailable, the service keeps the poll clock.
- `tests/qemu/alpine-shell.sh`: `wait_for_line` used `\r` in a `grep -E` pattern. GNU grep has no `\r` escape, so CRLF console lines never matched on Linux hosts. It now passes a literal CR.

`boot/efi/src/generated_boot.rs` is not included. The build regenerates it, so we left that to you.

## Evidence

Host: Linux x86-64 (CachyOS), Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, guests pinned to P-cores, QEMU 10.1.2 built from the release tarball, OVMF 2025.02, Rust 1.99.0. Docker Hub is about 220 ms RTT from here.

| Check | main 22d20a6 (pre-rebase) | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `make check` | pass | pass (also after rebase onto ecbb314) |
| `make test-alpine`, KVM | fail: SYN retransmits at 7, 21, 49, 104 ms; SYN-ACK at 220 ms gets RST | pass: one SYN, SYN-ACK accepted (also after rebase) |
| `make test-alpine`, TCG | not run | pass (also after rebase) |
| kernel forced to report unavailable, KVM | n/a | pass on the poll clock (timing-dependent) |
| `make benchmark-topology-matrix` + compare, KVM | stops at the first Ginux cell (pull) | completes, 9 runs per cell |

## Limitations

- Cross-processor TSC skew is not handled beyond a never-decreasing clamp, matching the Linux clock profile. QEMU does not advertise invariant TSC under `-cpu host` or `max`.
- Failures are now slower where the clock was fast: a silent peer costs up to 24.4 s per wait and a silent resolver about 10 s per DNS attempt, where KVM previously gave up within milliseconds.
- The DNS failures recorded in Gates 1 and 10 may share this cause, since smoltcp DNS retries use the same clock. We did not verify that.

The gate record in your HDAE format is below. We're happy to add it under `hdae/` if you want it in the tree.

<details><summary>Gate: Native Service Monotonic Clock</summary>

# Gate 34: Native Service Monotonic Clock

## Source

Found while collecting KVM benchmark data on Linux x86-64: every OCI registry
pull failed under KVM with "OCI registry TCP connection failed", while the same
pull passed under TCG.

## Goal

Give the native network service a real monotonic clock so smoltcp TCP and DNS
timers run in milliseconds rather than in poll iterations, and so registry
pulls work on fast hosts and over high-latency links.

## Approved scope

- Add native operation 39 that returns the kernel-calibrated timestamp-counter
  frequency, the same source the Linux clock profile already uses.
- Drive the registry network stack from RDTSC scaled by that frequency, with
  one charged call per registry session.
- Bound network waits by time instead of poll count, keeping the existing
  24.4-second bound.
- Keep the poll-count clock when the kernel reports the frequency unavailable.
- Repair the Alpine harness so CRLF console lines match under GNU grep.

## Non-goals

- No kvmclock, HPET, or other clock source.
- No change to Linux clock syscalls, timer interrupts, or the call budget.
- No change to QEMU CPU flags; invariant TSC stays unadvertised under
  `-cpu host` and `max`.
- No regenerated `boot/efi/src/generated_boot.rs`; the build regenerates
  it, so the maintainer does.

## Completed work

- [x] ABI constant, header, C conformance assertion, and frozen-contract test.
- [x] Kernel dispatch for operation 39.
- [x] Registry clock, session-wide monotonic clamp, and time-bounded waits.
- [x] `tests/qemu/alpine-shell.sh` CRLF match under GNU grep.

## Remaining work

- None.

## Acceptance criteria

- `make check` passes.
- Under KVM, an OCI pull across a 200+ ms RTT link completes where main fails.
- The KVM topology matrix and compare complete for Linux and Ginux cells.
- Under TCG, `make test-alpine` passes.
- A kernel that reports the frequency unavailable keeps the poll clock.

## Evidence

Host: Linux x86-64 (CachyOS), Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, guests pinned to
P-cores, QEMU 10.1.2 built from the release tarball, OVMF 2025.02, Rust
1.99.0, Docker Hub at about 220 ms RTT.

- `make check` passed.
- After rebasing onto `ecbb314`: `make check` and `make test-alpine` under
  KVM and TCG passed again.
- main `22d20a6` (before rebase), KVM, `make test-alpine`: failed. Capture shows SYN
  retransmits at 7, 21, 49 and 104 ms, the SYN-ACK at 220 ms answered with
  RST, three retries, then "OCI image pull failed".
- This branch, KVM and TCG, `make test-alpine`: passed (shell, restart, and
  failure containment). Capture shows one SYN and the 220 ms SYN-ACK accepted.
- Before the harness repair, the branch completed the pull and the runtime
  suite but timed out waiting for `alpine: failed`, which was present with a
  CRLF ending.
- Kernel forced to return unavailable, KVM: `make test-alpine` passed on the
  poll clock (SYN retransmits at 25, 74 and 172 ms). That pass depends on the
  per-poll cost and is not a property of the poll clock.
- `make benchmark-topology-matrix` and `make benchmark-topology-compare`
  completed under KVM with 9 runs per cell. The results are not part of this
  change and will follow separately.

## Decisions and limitations

The service reads RDTSC directly instead of calling the kernel for each
reading because a native service has a 23-call budget renewed only by progress
calls; a per-poll call would exhaust it. CR4.TSD is not set, so RDTSC is
already available in ring 3 and the operation grants no new capability.

An unknown operation returns `u64::MAX`, which the entry stub treats as
terminating the caller, so a service cannot probe for the operation. This is
safe because services ship in the same boot image as the kernel.

Time is clamped to never decrease within a session. Cross-processor TSC skew
is not otherwise handled; this matches the existing Linux clock profile. A
service migrated to a processor whose counter is far ahead would latch that
time for the rest of the session and expire its waits early.

Failures are now slower where the clock was fast: a silent peer costs up to
24.4 seconds per wait and a silent resolver up to about 10 seconds per DNS
attempt in real time, where KVM previously gave up within milliseconds.

Each wait checks the socket before the deadline on every poll, as the
poll-bounded loops did, and DNS refreshes the interface time before starting
a query, because smoltcp stamps the query timeout from the last poll.

The previous code also restarted the TCP clock at zero for each connection
after DNS had advanced the interface clock. A single session clock removes
that backwards step.

Earlier registry failures recorded in Gates 1 and 10 were DNS timeouts. They
may share this cause, since smoltcp DNS retries use the same clock, but that
was not verified.

## Delivery strategy

- Working branch: `fix/native-timestamp-frequency`.
- Intended base: `main` at `ecbb314`.
- Pull request: one pull request from `CG-8663/ginux`.
- Actual commits: `586de64` repairs the harness; `2c36711` adds the clock.

## Review policy and outcome

An independent review found no blocking defects; its deadline-ordering, DNS
timestamp, and Instant-range findings are fixed. Pending maintainer review.

</details>
